title: The flame in Nataraja's hand
hookLine: in Kashi, where cremation fires burn day and night, tradition says Shiva whispers freedom to the dying; the flame in Nataraja's hand, and why Shaivas wear ash
carry: samhara: the ending is god's work too
tomorrow: why does one hand point at his foot?

lines: A FLAME IN THE UPPER LEFT HAND.
cards: In Varanasi, which Hindus also call Kashi, there's a cremation ground on the bank of the Ganga called Manikarnika. People say its fires haven't gone out in centuries.
Families carry their dead down the steps, day and night.

And tradition tells something remarkable about this place: here, Shiva himself bends to the ear of each person who dies, and whispers the mantra of crossing over, and they are set free. Now look at Nataraja.
Opposite the drum, in his upper left hand, held in an open palm, is a flame.

teach.b: In the usual reading of the image, the flame is samhara, dissolution. Things are made, last a while, and are drawn back in.

teach.h: DRUM AND FLAME AT THE SAME HEIGHT.
teach.b: Look where the classic bronzes put it: drum on one side, flame on the other, both at the same height, neither higher, neither dropped. The beginning in one hand, the ending in the other. That's a big Hindu teaching.
Time turns in great cycles; the Puranas say that at the end of a great cycle the worlds are drawn back in, and in time made again. And the ending is as much God's work as the beginning.
So Shiva's fire isn't the enemy of life. In Kashi, it's where freedom is whispered. And remember who holds it: the groom smeared with ash, the god of the cremation ground.
That's why many Shaiva Hindus wear vibhuti, sacred ash, often in three lines across the forehead.
Many read it this way: everything burns down to this, and Shiva wears it like clothing, because what he is can't burn. And families still carry a loved one's ashes to the Ganga, many to Kashi itself.

Then the week, looked back on: Parvati's tapas, a wedding, three cities, the lord who is half woman, a saint at the dancer's feet, the drum, and now the flame. A grandmother dies, a job ends, a childhood home is sold.

teach.h: THE ENDING IS GOD'S WORK TOO.
teach.b: The flame in Nataraja's hand says the ending is held too, by the same hand that keeps the beat.

how: In Nataraja images the upper left hand holds a flame, read as dissolution, balanced against the drum of creation; many Shaiva Hindus wear vibhuti, sacred ash, on the forehead, and families bring the ashes of the dead to the Ganga, many to Kashi itself.

o: a lamp waved before a god at the close of worship
a torch Shiva carries to burn down demon cities
Shiva the dancer, here the flame of endings in his left hand

games.q: the flame and the ash — tap the pairs.
p: sacred ash, worn on the forehead
Kashi's cremation ground on the Ganga

s: Nataraja holds the flame as a weapon
it rests in an open palm, read as samhara, dissolution, the ending.
in the classic bronzes, the drum and the flame are held at the same height
balanced across the shoulders: neither the beginning nor the ending is set above the other.
tradition says Shiva whispers a mantra of crossing to those who die in Kashi
it's why so many Hindus hope to die in Kashi, Shiva's city.

games.q: you're the sculptor. one upper hand holds the drum of beginning, the other the flame of ending. how do you place them?
o: the drum high, the flame low.
the flame high, the drum low.
games.why: in the classic bronzes both are raised to the same height, balanced like the pans of a scale. neither beginning nor ending is set above the other.

practice: Rest your hands on your knees, palms up: into the right palm put something beginning in your life, and into the left something that's ending, or needs to. Let both hands rest at the same height and breathe with both.
If you keep vibhuti, you can touch a little to your forehead; if you pray, offer both hands to Shiva, or to God, with Om Namah Shivaya. If you don't pray, simply hold both, level.

wordCard.voice: Nataraja explained. Today, the flame in his upper left hand: samhara, the ending, held level with the drum's beginning, both part of the same dance.
